doc.title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal Interview, 1962-05-24

title: Her daughter, a former nun, composes music
summary: Edna describes her daughter in Richmond who was a nun for four years and composed music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, now that's about all the music I know from there. But I tell you, I have something. I have a sheet music that my daughter composed. But I wouldn't want her, I wouldn't want you to write to her. And involve her in it. Well, you could hear her. No, no, it made her sick the last time. You see, she has seven books. She lives in Richmond, Virginia. She was one time a nun. She was a nun for four years in the convent. And she, well, they give you six years to make up your mind. Every year they give you. And you can sign or not sign. So, oh, I thought, sure. And then she had gone to Rock Castle in Virginia at school. You know her at school? Color school, Rock Castle, Virginia. Girls only. Well, she had a scholarship and she went there. And so when she came back, oh, I thought, sure, she was going to teach her something. Because, oh, had this priest here at Corpus Christi. Corpus Christi had a job waiting for her to teach. And had so many plans and everything. She had wrote several times, jokingly, that she was going to wear a veil. Mother, you'd be surprised if you see me wearing a veil when I come home. You know, that way. And I wouldn't. I said, oh, she's just joking. She's not. So finally when she came home, I said, Melda, what are you going to do? She finished, graduated, you know. She said, Imelda, what's her name? Imelda Sarendra. She says, I don't know. She says, I think I'm going to the convent. She says, I can't then. She says, yes, Mother, I think I'm going. I said, well, you know, it's up to you. But all those years of study and all that. And I said, then you're in the convent. She said, well, they need teachers. They need teachers in the convent. They need smart. They don't need only scrub women in the convent. They need people like me to help them out. I says, but not you. I said, they need people like you, but not you. Oh, she says, yes, Mother, they do. Don't feel like that. And so I said, well, not going to say far again. So she just went on. She stole away one day and went to the convent. And so she stayed in there four years and came out. Now I was so satisfied to have her in there then. I made up her mind, you know. But then she came out and had seven boys. Imagine, came out and had seven boys. And wonderful, seven wonderful boys. Wonderful. All kinds of ways. Two of them in there. Two are in there. Two are in there. She must have had a love. All boys, not even a girl. Every time she said, Mother, this is going to be a girl. I just know it. I just know it. Come a boy. And so she just wrote me a letter yesterday. I got this letter. Say, Mother, try to come over in June. The boys are going to be here. And let's make it more merry. You and part Senegal come over and we'll have a house full. And we'll have a merry time. So, to get in now, get back to this. After she got out of the town, then she started having children. I guess too close together. They were about a year apart. And she got nervous. She was terribly nervous. So nervous that I had her husband. But she had a wonderful family. His family. And he was a wonderful man to her. He still is. And an old lady was an Indian type of old lady. She was half Indian. As I say, this mixture. But she had more Indian blood in her than anything else. And she was just wonderful to her. She said, Ms. Senegal, don't worry. When you're gone, I'm her mother. And, well, she took this nervous breakdown. They had to send for me. I went over there and got her and brought her here. And I brought her to, I had, by sewing, I knew so many rich white people that could help me. And they knew this, uh, doctor, uh, Hotel Dieu, that famous doctor, metal doctor, Hotel Dieu. Oh, yes, indeed. They brought me, um, the noise even had her going there just with all the people. No segregation. You know, they said, you bring Melda in there and just say, we sent her there. And so we were treated just like anybody else. And he just took, oh, he just took so much patience with her. And when I told him about the children, oh, he said, what a pity a beautiful woman like that. And all these boys to live for her. And, um, and the thing of it, she didn't think she was nervous. And she didn't look nervous. And to look at her, you wouldn't think she was nervous. But it was inside. That's what the doctor said, it was inward, you know. And she was holding it all in. Smart. Oh, she was smart as she can be. So finally the doctor told her, he said, um, he says, well, you're nervous, my dear child. He says, no doctor, I am not nervous. He says, yes, you are nervous. He says, yes, you are nervous. I said, well, how can you tell? He says, I can tell. He said, can you tell me why I'm nervous or how? He says, because you are nervous. He told the nurse to go get a glass of water. And he says, now, if you can hold that glass of water still, as I do, then you'll know you're nervous. I said, oh, you're nervous. All right. She said, all right. You got to get a glass of water. So she says, you hold it first. I said, you hold it. Oh, I said, oh, Mel is shaking my goodness. Tell the doctor what to do. And so he held the water and he was holding it and it was shaking, you know, just shaking a little bit. She says, now, doctor, can't you see it shaking? He says, oh, no, I'm just a little upset. He said, but it's not shaking. I'm a little upset. But he said, she said, doctor, but you see it shaking, don't you? He said, a little upset, that's all. I said, now you do it. She took the place and held it up. Just as still, not even a quiver. So she said, now, who is nervous? You are. I mean, it was something. So he said, well, all right, we compromise on that. You just come see me a couple of times. We'll find out who's nervous. I'm nervous or you're nervous. So to get back to this, she had this nervous breakdown. And during her sickness, she wrote the most beautiful poems. I'm going to get this to show you now. But I don't want it to, I don't want you to write to her about it. Because I don't want it to go back, you know, into that nervous state, you know.
You ought to get our music too.
You're not nervous because she wrote all that. Yeah. Well, we've got about a second left.
